variants.title: Trace the online request
variants.context: An online NLP request crosses five stages: admission bounds the work, representation versions the input, scheduling protects the deadline, inference executes the pinned artifact, and the decision stage applies product policy. The request identity and its representation version travel with it the whole way.
variants.prompt: A moderation endpoint receives one short comment under a 200 ms deadline. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Normalize the text and tokenize it with the pinned vocabulary, recording any truncation.
Calibrate, validate the output shape, apply safety rules, and return, abstain, or escalate.
Authenticate the caller, validate the format, enforce the token and deadline limits, and assign a request ID.
Group the request with compatible work inside the token budget and cap its queue age.
Run the pinned model and precision profile, keeping scores, stop reason, latency, and errors.

variants.hint: Which stage is the only one that can refuse the request before any work is spent?
variants.explanation: Admission bounds the work before it becomes expensive, and the decision stage owns the product answer rather than the raw model output.

variants.title: Trace the online request
variants.context: An online NLP request crosses five stages: admission bounds the work, representation versions the input, scheduling protects the deadline, inference executes the pinned artifact, and the decision stage applies product policy. The request identity and its representation version travel with it the whole way.
variants.prompt: A 9,000 token support ticket is chunked instead of rejected. Put the stages in order for the chunked request.

items.text: Representation chunks the text with the pinned tokenizer and records every chunk boundary.
Scheduling admits the chunks inside the token budget and caps how long they may wait.
Admission validates the format, enforces the deadline, and assigns one request ID to the whole ticket.
The decision stage aggregates the chunk results, applies policy, and returns one answer or abstains.
Inference runs the pinned model on each chunk and preserves its scores and stop reason.

variants.hint: The chunk boundaries have to be recorded before anything can be aggregated.
variants.explanation: Chunking is a representation decision and aggregation is a decision-stage responsibility, which is why both boundaries are versioned rather than hidden inside model code.

variants.title: Trace the online request
variants.context: An online NLP request crosses five stages: admission bounds the work, representation versions the input, scheduling protects the deadline, inference executes the pinned artifact, and the decision stage applies product policy. The request identity and its representation version travel with it the whole way.
variants.prompt: A streaming summarizer must cancel cleanly when the caller disconnects. Put the stages in order, ending with the cancellation.

items.text: Inference streams output tokens while the stop reason and latency are recorded.
Admission assigns the request ID and the deadline that every later stage will be measured against.
The decision stage stops generation, releases the scheduled tokens, and records the cancellation.
Representation tokenizes the prompt and records the input length that the prefill will pay for.
Scheduling reserves a token budget slot and starts counting queue age against the deadline.

variants.hint: Cancellation frees something that a specific earlier stage handed out.
variants.explanation: A cancellation is a first-class scheduler and policy event, so the deadline assigned at admission is what every later stage spends and what cancellation reclaims.

variants.title: Release one compatible bundle
variants.context: Representation, model, and policy are released as one compatible bundle: freeze the input semantics, package weights with runtime, calibration, thresholds, and safety rules, gate by slice offline and in shadow, then canary with an automatic stop and the prior bundle still deployable.
variants.prompt: A new intent classifier is ready to ship. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Canary with automatic guardrail stops while the prior compatible bundle stays deployable.
Pin normalization, language routing, tokenizer files, vocabulary, maximum length, and truncation policy.
Compare quality, abstention, latency, and error cost across languages, length buckets, and known hard cases.
Version the weights, runtime and precision, calibration, labels, thresholds, and safety rules together.

variants.hint: Which artifact decides what the model even sees?
variants.explanation: Input semantics are frozen first because every later comparison is only valid if both sides tokenize the same text the same way.

variants.title: Release one compatible bundle
variants.context: Representation, model, and policy are released as one compatible bundle: freeze the input semantics, package weights with runtime, calibration, thresholds, and safety rules, gate by slice offline and in shadow, then canary with an automatic stop and the prior bundle still deployable.
variants.prompt: Only a normalization rule changes and the weights are untouched. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Repackage the same weights, thresholds, and safety rules against that new representation version.
Canary the bundle with rollback to the previous representation and model pair.
Gate the pair by slice, because a normalization change can move the decision boundary on its own.
Version the new normalization rule as a representation change with its own identifier.

variants.hint: Ask what moved, and then ask what that movement can change downstream.
variants.explanation: Changing one side of the contract still changes decisions, so a representation-only edit ships through the same gate and rollback path as new weights.

variants.title: Release one compatible bundle
variants.context: Representation, model, and policy are released as one compatible bundle: freeze the input semantics, package weights with runtime, calibration, thresholds, and safety rules, gate by slice offline and in shadow, then canary with an automatic stop and the prior bundle still deployable.
variants.prompt: An incident requires returning to the last known good behavior. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Restore the matching weights, thresholds, and safety rules alongside it.
Identify the bundle version that produced the last known good decisions.
Replay quarantined and in-flight jobs idempotently from an explicit checkpoint.
Restore its representation so tokens recover their previous meaning.

variants.hint: Restoring weights under a newer tokenizer is not a rollback.
variants.explanation: Rollback moves the whole representation, model, and policy bundle, and replay is safe only once the restored bundle is the one interpreting the inputs.

variants.title: Turn tokens into replicas
variants.context: Request count hides the work in an NLP service. Token demand is requests per second times tokens per request, and the replica floor is that demand divided by measured per-replica token throughput at a deliberately safe utilization target, rounded up.
variants.prompt: A classification service takes 300 requests per second and each request schedules 800 tokens. The measured profile sustains 12,000 tokens per second per replica, and the utilization target is 60 percent. What is the replica floor?
variants.hint: Measured throughput is a peak, not a number you are allowed to plan against.
variants.explanation: Demand is 300 times 800, which is 240,000 tokens per second; safe capacity is 12,000 times 0.6, which is 7,200; 240,000 divided by 7,200 is 33.3, and the floor rounds up to 34.

mistakes.feedback: 20 divides by the full 12,000 tokens per second and ignores the 60 percent utilization target.
33 is the exact quotient truncated; the replica floor rounds up so the last fraction of demand has somewhere to run.

variants.title: Turn tokens into replicas
variants.context: Request count hides the work in an NLP service. Token demand is requests per second times tokens per request, and the replica floor is that demand divided by measured per-replica token throughput at a deliberately safe utilization target, rounded up.
variants.prompt: A summarizer serves 40 requests per second with 1,500 input tokens and 200 output tokens each. The generator profile sustains 4,200 tokens per second per replica at a 70 percent utilization target. What is the replica floor?
variants.hint: A generator pays for the prompt and for every token it writes.
variants.explanation: Each request schedules 1,700 tokens, so demand is 68,000 tokens per second; safe capacity is 4,200 times 0.7, which is 2,940; 68,000 divided by 2,940 is 23.1, rounded up to 24.

mistakes.feedback: 17 uses the raw 4,200 tokens per second and leaves no utilization headroom.
21 counts only the 1,500 input tokens and forgets that output tokens are scheduled work too.

variants.title: Turn tokens into replicas
variants.context: Request count hides the work in an NLP service. Token demand is requests per second times tokens per request, and the replica floor is that demand divided by measured per-replica token throughput at a deliberately safe utilization target, rounded up.
variants.prompt: Peak traffic reaches 600 requests per second at 500 tokens each. The compact encoder sustains 28,000 tokens per second per replica and the team plans at a 75 percent utilization target. What is the replica floor?
variants.hint: Do the demand side first, then shrink what one replica may be credited with.
variants.explanation: Demand is 300,000 tokens per second; safe capacity is 28,000 times 0.75, which is 21,000; 300,000 divided by 21,000 is 14.3, rounded up to 15.

mistakes.feedback: 11 plans against benchmark peak throughput rather than the 75 percent target.
14 truncates instead of rounding up and leaves part of peak demand unplaced.

variants.title: Answer the boundary violation
variants.context: Each boundary in the path has one explicit response when it is violated. Input over the contract is rejected, chunked, or routed to an asynchronous job; exhausted capacity sheds low-priority work and caps queue age; drift isolates the slice and rolls back the whole bundle.
variants.prompt: A 40 page contract is posted to a synchronous extraction endpoint whose ceiling is 4,000 tokens. What is the correct response?
options: Raise the token ceiling for this tenant so the document fits the request.
Truncate to the first 4,000 tokens and return the extraction as usual.
Reject it, or route it to the asynchronous path with job identity and progress.
optionFeedback: Raising the ceiling changes the deadline and memory math for every request on that path.
Silent truncation discards decisive text while the response still looks like a normal answer.
Correct: oversize input is rejected, chunked, or moved to a job that can outlive the request.
variants.hint: Which option leaves the caller unaware that evidence was dropped?
variants.explanation: Input over the contract must produce an explicit outcome, because never silently discarding decisive text is what keeps the decision meaningful.

variants.title: Answer the boundary violation
variants.context: Each boundary in the path has one explicit response when it is violated. Input over the contract is rejected, chunked, or routed to an asynchronous job; exhausted capacity sheds low-priority work and caps queue age; drift isolates the slice and rolls back the whole bundle.
variants.prompt: Online capacity is exhausted at peak and queue age is climbing past the deadline. What is the correct response?
options: Shed low-priority work, cap queue age, or move traffic to a validated smaller model.
Increase the maximum batch wait, since larger batches raise token throughput.
Keep admitting everything so the added latency is shared evenly across callers.
optionFeedback: Correct: overload is answered by admitting less or serving cheaper, both of which are quality decisions made in advance.
Batch wait is spent from the same end-to-end deadline, so a longer wait makes the miss worse.
Sharing the delay evenly means every caller misses the deadline instead of some of them being told no.
variants.hint: Every option costs someone something; ask which cost was budgeted.
variants.explanation: An exhausted online path sheds or degrades deliberately, because unbounded queues turn a capacity problem into a deadline problem for everyone.

variants.title: Answer the boundary violation
variants.context: Each boundary in the path has one explicit response when it is violated. Input over the contract is rejected, chunked, or routed to an asynchronous job; exhausted capacity sheds low-priority work and caps queue age; drift isolates the slice and rolls back the whole bundle.
variants.prompt: Two days after a deployment, quality on long documents in one language falls below its threshold while the global score looks fine. What is the correct response?
options: Isolate the slice, halt promotion, and roll back the representation, model, and policy together.
Roll back only the model weights and keep the newer tokenizer in production.
Raise the abstention rate for that language until more labels arrive next month.
optionFeedback: Correct: drift is contained by slice and reversed as one bundle, since the pieces are only valid together.
Weights restored under a different tokenizer create a pairing that was never gated on any slice.
Abstaining hides the regression behind a lower answer rate without restoring the behavior users lost.
variants.hint: Ask which artifacts were gated together in the first place.
variants.explanation: A regression on one slice is enough to stop a rollout, and the rollback returns the whole compatible bundle rather than one of its parts.

variants.title: Name what each part pins
variants.context: An NLP architecture is a set of named contracts, signal families, and workload shapes, and each one pins something different. Confusing them is how a team ships a fast service that answers the wrong question.
variants.prompt: Match each written contract to what it fixes for the service.

pairs.label: Input contract
pairs.detail: Supported languages, formats, maximum tokens, privacy class, and malformed-input behavior.

pairs.label: Decision contract
pairs.detail: Output schema, confidence or abstention rule, policy checks, and human override rights.

pairs.label: Service contract
pairs.detail: Traffic distribution, deadline, freshness, availability, and the cost ceiling.

pairs.label: Learning contract
pairs.detail: Outcome signal, evaluation slices, retraining trigger, and audit retention.

variants.hint: One contract is about what may come in, one about what may go out.
variants.explanation: The four contracts are written before the architecture, because each one constrains a different part of the path and none of them can substitute for another.

variants.title: Name what each part pins
variants.context: An NLP architecture is a set of named contracts, signal families, and workload shapes, and each one pins something different. Confusing them is how a team ships a fast service that answers the wrong question.
variants.prompt: Match each monitoring signal family to what it reveals.

pairs.label: Traffic and shape
pairs.detail: Requests and tokens per second plus input and output length distributions.

pairs.label: System behavior
pairs.detail: Queue age, batch fill, memory pressure, timeouts, cancellations, and fallback rate.

pairs.label: Decision behavior
pairs.detail: Score distribution, abstention, class mix, output length, and schema failures.

pairs.label: Outcome quality
pairs.detail: Delayed labels, human corrections, appeals, and slice-specific regressions.

variants.hint: Ask whether the number describes the input, the machine, the answer, or the consequence.
variants.explanation: Latency without quality can reward a broken fallback and quality without traffic data can hide who never received an answer, so all four families are watched together.

variants.title: Name what each part pins
variants.context: An NLP architecture is a set of named contracts, signal families, and workload shapes, and each one pins something different. Confusing them is how a team ships a fast service that answers the wrong question.
variants.prompt: Match each NLP workload to the property that dominates its design.

pairs.label: Classify or extract
pairs.detail: Maps text to a small bounded result and can batch inputs of similar length.

pairs.label: Retrieve or rank
pairs.detail: Depends on an index whose embedding model, tokenizer, and corpus version stay compatible.

pairs.label: Generate text
pairs.detail: Pays for input prefill and then for each output token, so streaming and cancellation are controls.

variants.hint: Ask what the output size does to the cost of one request.
variants.explanation: Naming the decision before the model is what makes the deadline, the batching strategy, and the failure behavior derivable rather than guessed.
